content.content:
Haj-Wan: "I wait for Sei-Wan, my kin. He walked out into the basin alone, to prove himself to the Agaceph, and he has not come back. I am Agaceph too. By our custom none of us may follow a walk-out, so I stay at this gate. An outsider may follow him. He went east from the gate through the shallows, and he is up among the roots there. Vipers lie in the roots, and the mud holds anyone who stands still. Nothing that walks in the basin lives long. Gih-Xaleel, the levy warden beside me, will say the same. I want him alive. He wants the walk-out to count, and it counts only if he comes home on his own feet. If another brings him in, the Agaceph will say he did not finish. I would have him alive and shamed sooner than proud and dead. Bring him home if you must. But if he can walk, let the walk-out be his own."

content.content:
the levy warden: "No. I keep this gate, and what a tribe does with its own young is for that tribe to do. The levy has never stood in the way of a rite, and I will not stand in your way. Sei-Wan went out into the basin days ago, and he is not back. Haj-Wan, who waits beside me, will tell you why he went. If you go after him, I will not stop you. But hear this. What lies in the reed roots bites, and what it bites dies. The levy will not come in after you, so you go alone. I do not like what the rite costs. I watch young ones walk out here and I do not follow, because the levy keeps to the gate. When one does not come back, I have stood here and watched."
